Фиолетовая точка — запрос,

#### Candidate queues and the stopping rule The authors distinguish the result count from the search width: > ```ef``` - the size of the dynamic list for the nearest neighbors (used during the search). Higher ```ef``` > leads to more accurate but slower search. ```ef``` cannot be set lower than the number of queried nearest neighbors > ```k```. The value ```ef``` of can be anything between ```k``` and the size of the dataset. *hnswlib authors, [HNSW algorithm parameters, v0.8.0](https://github.com/nmslib/hnswlib/blob/3f3429661187e4c24a490a0f148fc6bc89042b3d/ALGO_PARAMS.md). Original English retained; [Apache-2.0](/licenses/hnswlib-3f342966-Apache-2.0.txt).* At the base layer, keep two priority queues. The frontier contains vertices whose adjacency lists may still be inspected, with the closest vertex first. The result queue retains at most `ef` current best vertices, with the farthest one available for removal. A visited set prevents repeated distance calculations for vertices reached through several edges. Start both queues with the entry vertex. Pop the closest frontier candidate and inspect its previously unseen neighbors. A neighbor enters the queues if the result queue is not full or it is closer than the current worst result. If the result queue grows beyond `ef`, remove its farthest member. The two queues serve different purposes: a vertex removed from the results can still have a pending frontier entry. For the unfiltered, no-deletion search used here, stop when the closest remaining frontier candidate is farther than the worst retained result and the result queue is full. This is an approximate stopping rule. A far frontier vertex can still have an edge to a very close, unseen vertex; its own distance is not a lower bound on all vertices reachable through it. Return to the chain above and use squared L2 distances. From query 0, the distances to A, B and C are 16, 25 and 0.01. | Width / expansion | Result queue and next step | | --- | --- | | `ef=1`, A | A: 16. Reject B: 25; the frontier becomes empty. | | `ef=2`, A | A: 16, B: 25. Keep B because the result queue has space. | | `ef=2`, B | C: 0.01, A: 16. Discover C and remove B from results. | | `ef=2`, C | C: 0.01, A: 16. No unseen neighbors; return C for `k=1`. | The wider search expands three vertices even though `ef=2`. The width limits retained results, not the total number of distance calculations or expansions. The final response can still contain just one neighbor. The implementation below follows the two-queue logic in [hnswlib `searchBaseLayerST`](https://github.com/nmslib/hnswlib/blob/3f3429661187e4c24a490a0f148fc6bc89042b3d/hnswlib/hnswalg.h#L311). It uses a supplied one-dimensional graph to expose the search steps. It does not implement insertion, upper layers, deletion, filtering or the optimized memory layout of hnswlib. The Python code and worked graph are Bookvar teaching additions, not a performance measurement of the library. ```python import heapq import math def search_layer_demo(points, graph, query, entry, ef, k=1): if (not isinstance(ef, int) or isinstance(ef, bool) or not isinstance(k, int) or isinstance(k, bool) or not 1 <= k <= ef): raise ValueError("need integer 1 <= k <= ef") if entry not in points or set(points) != set(graph): raise ValueError("need an entry and an adjacency list for every vertex") if not math.isfinite(query) or any(not math.isfinite(x) for x in points.values()): raise ValueError("need finite one-dimensional coordinates") if any(v not in points for neighbors in graph.values() for v in neighbors): raise ValueError("every edge must point to a known vertex") distance = lambda v: (points[v] - query) ** 2 frontier = [(distance(entry), entry)] # nearest unexpanded first best = [(-distance(entry), entry)] # farthest retained first visited, expanded = {entry}, [] while frontier: d, vertex = heapq.heappop(frontier) if len(best) == ef and d > -best[0][0]: break expanded.append(vertex) for neighbor in graph[vertex]: if neighbor in visited: continue visited.add(neighbor) dn = distance(neighbor) if len(best) < ef or dn < -best[0][0]: heapq.heappush(frontier, (dn, neighbor)) heapq.heappush(best, (-dn, neighbor)) if len(best) > ef: heapq.heappop(best) return sorted((-d, v) for d, v in best)[:k], visited, expanded points = {"A": 4., "B": 5., "C": .1} graph = {"A": ["B"], "B": ["A", "C"], "C": ["B"]} narrow, _, _ = search_layer_demo(points, graph, 0., "A", ef=1) wide, visited, expanded = search_layer_demo(points, graph, 0., "A", ef=2) assert narrow[0][1] == "A" and wide[0][1] == "C" assert visited == set(points) and expanded == ["A", "B", "C"] assert len(expanded) > 2 # ef is not a hard limit on graph expansions assert math.isclose(wide[0][0], .01) ``` Increasing the width cannot create a missing graph connection. If a component containing the true nearest neighbor is unreachable from the entry, even a width equal to the whole database cannot reach it. The graph structure and entry selection therefore affect recall separately from the query-time width. Returning to all IVF lists has a different property: with IVFFlat it explicitly visits the complete database. #### Why construction does not keep only the closest links In hnswlib, [getNeighborsByHeuristic2](https://github.com/nmslib/hnswlib/blob/3f3429661187e4c24a490a0f148fc6bc89042b3d/hnswlib/hnswalg.h#L443) considers candidate neighbors in increasing distance from the new vertex. After accepting a neighbor, it can reject another candidate that is closer to an already accepted neighbor than to the new vertex. The candidate may provide a redundant route through the same nearby region. For a new vertex at 0 and candidates A=1, B=1.1 and C=−1.2, the two closest candidates are A and B. With a two-link budget, the heuristic first accepts A. It rejects B because the A–B distance is 0.1, smaller than B's distance 1.1 from the new vertex. It then accepts C: the A–C distance 2.2 exceeds C's distance 1.2 from the new vertex. The two links point to opposite sides rather than the same tight group. The actual code compares the configured distance function; squared L2 gives the same decisions in this example. This local heuristic does not guarantee a globally optimal graph or complete connectivity. `efConstruction` controls the candidate search used while adding vertices; `M` limits the retained connections. A wide construction search and a large connection budget change different parts of the graph-building procedure. ### Product quantization: код вместо координат
